_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 8 Computers Everywhere. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js with the scenes named in renderer below. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the scenes refuse to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. Written for a Grade 1 child: short sentences, the lesson's own words (program, app, input, output, control, robot), the lesson's own examples (Grandma's call, the lions, the six programs, the eight devices, the hidden computers, the robots and the bicycle). Read README.md in this folder before rendering without --dry, --preview or --draft: a real render buys narration.
title: Computers Everywhere
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Know that there are a range of computer systems with different functions, including communication, entertainment, creativity, research and for controlling other technology.
Know that computers can run many different programs, including games, apps and document creation tools.
Know that information and data can be input to computers in many different ways.
Know that computers can output information in many different ways.
Know that there are many everyday devices that use computers to control what they do.
Identify what robots are and where they may be found in the real world.

beats.say: Look around you. Computers are everywhere.
Some are easy to see. Some are hiding inside other things.
A computer is a machine that runs programs. Computers come in lots of sizes.
A desktop, a laptop, a tablet and a smartphone. All four are computers.
People use computers for lots of different jobs. Here are five.
Talking to Grandma far away. That is communication.
Watching a film, or playing a game. That is entertainment.
Drawing a picture, or making music. That is creativity.
Finding out about lions. That is research.
And controlling other machines, like a washing machine. That is control.
One tablet can run lots of different programs. A program on a tablet is called an app.
Open Paint, and you can draw.
Open the ball game, and you can play.
Open Writing, and you can type a story.
Videos plays films. Call rings Grandma. Search finds things out.
Six programs, and just one computer. A computer can run many programs.
A computer needs information to work with. It goes in through an input.
A keyboard puts letters in. A mouse puts in your pointing and clicking.
A microphone puts your voice in. A camera puts a picture in.
When you tap a touchscreen, your tap goes in too.
Then the computer gives information out, through an output.
A screen shows words and pictures. A speaker plays sounds.
A printer puts them on paper. Lights can flash to tell you something.
A touchscreen is both. Your tap goes in, and the picture comes out.
A computer does not have to look like a computer. Lots of everyday machines have a small one hiding inside.
A washing machine has one. It controls the wash: fill, wash, spin.
Traffic lights have one. It decides when each light changes.
A microwave, a car, a watch and a TV have one too.
A spoon, a book and a candle have none. Nothing inside them decides what they do.
A robot is a machine with a computer inside. Its program makes it move and do a job.
In a factory, a robot arm builds cars.
At home, a robot vacuum cleans the floor, then goes back to charge.
On Mars, a rover drives about and takes pictures.
Robots also work in hospitals and warehouses, and even under the sea.
Most robots do not look like people at all.
A bicycle moves too, but it is not a robot. It moves because you pedal it.
So now you know. Computers do lots of jobs, and one computer can run many programs.
Information goes in, and it comes out. And computers hide inside everyday things.
A robot has a computer inside that makes it move.
Now go and find the computers around you.
